New Moon Cape Cod Canal Report with AJ Coots of Red Top | August Fishing Report

AJ Coots of Red Top Sporting Goods in Buzzards Bay joins Kevin Collins for a new moon canal report on August 12th. After a slow stretch, the canal is waking up — slot and above-slot fish on morning minus tides, topwater action at daybreak, bonito spotted in the canal and Cape Cod Bay, a sailfish off Chatham, and a full Buzzards Bay bottom fish update. Plus AJ breaks down exactly which plugs to pack for a squid bite vs. a mackerel bite, and a Saturday showcase on August 15th you don't want to miss.

Cape Cod Bay Bass & Bluefin with Sam Mullen of the Goose Hummock | Early August Fishing Report

Sam Mullen of the Goose Hummock in Orleans joins Kevin Collins for an early August fishing report covering Cape Cod Bay and beyond. Cape Cod Bay is still the star of the show for striped bass — and the squid bite is still ripping. Bluefish are finally filtering in. Bonito have arrived in the bay. And Sam shares the incredible story of landing a 485-pound giant bluefin on a 21-foot center console. Plus a full bottom fish update: fluke, sea bass, and the late-season sea bass extension through October 14th.

all_videos_in_window.title: Bass Attack a Paddletail Underwater (Slowed Down 80%)
all_videos_in_window.description:
Just a little more Monomoy Tackle paddletail action for ya. Filmed earlier this summer off Wellfleet onboard one of our weekly MFCC trips with Flatliner Charters. These bass were moving fast, so we slowed the footage down by as much as 80% — at real speed, these strikes happen in the blink of an eye.

A few people have asked how we got this one — I used a WaterWolf in-line camera with the paddletail rigged about 3 feet out in front of it. Tyler would bring me right up to the blitzes, I would cast towards the edge of the commotion, and reel the paddle at a pretty fast clip since the bass were really focused on the surface. 

Wish I could take credit for perfect timing, but a lot of this comes down to getting lucky and being in the right place at the right time. 🎣

Tight lines! 🎣

Ryan

all_videos_in_window.title: August 6th 2026 New England Video Fishing Forecast with Dave Anderson
all_videos_in_window.description:
After a brief showing in early July, the bonito are back and it seems like they’re here to stay, this time. A strong push of bones swung into the South County shoreline and moved east, with strong catches along the entire Rhody shoreline and up into Buzzards Bay. We also saw a continuation of the increasing fluke bite with good reports from Block Island, eastern Long Island Sound, Nantucket Sound and even some good reports from Duxbury Bay. Striper action continues to hold strong, but shark depredation remains a major issue throughout southern New England.

all_videos_in_window.title: August 6th, 2026 New Jersey/Delaware Bay Fishing Report with Jim Hutchinson, Jr.
all_videos_in_window.description: Some quality fluke reported out of the Shark River Inlet fleet in the past week is evidence enough of an improving bite out along the inshore sticky stuff.  We'll run down a few of the latest catches reported back to us here at The Fisherman Magazine for the New Jersey, Delaware Bay region, with fluke, sheepshead, and blowfish, perhaps backed up with a steamer-full of little necks (6:40).  Run through the August editorial lineup in the magazine, and our digital weekly (10:12) with an overview of this week's Next Cast and the connection between rays, cobia and bluefin tuna along with the latest offshore intel from Canyon Runner.  Our lead image of the week (22:10) puts a husband and wife in the right spot at the time for their wedding anniversary and a blitz of bluefish at Sandy Hook as we …

Uh we've we've seen a lot of uh lot of nice-sized bones coming in. Guys in the on the shore, guys in the boats, guys in the kayaks. Uh it really it kind of just happened all at once. Um middle of middle of the week last week. It's been moving from the western half of Rhode Island and heading east. And uh it's been a really it's been a strong fishery over these last several days. And uh it's got a lot of guys up here fired up for hardtail season. And uh already hearing from tackle shops that, you know, epoxy jigs and XO jigs and all the things that you would expect are starting to fly off the shelves in anticipation of uh more excitement surrounding that species and hopefully a maybe a strong albie season come the end of the month here. So, uh that's been cool. I don't know, do you guys get bonito in the summertime, Jim? >> Yeah, we do. In fact, some of the uh some of the boats are starting to target them. Um you know, we had in in years past, we've had bonito in close right along the beach into October into November. >> Um same here. >> so, that's really cool. We haven't really had a great bonito run inshore like that in a few years. But yeah, the boats that are are going out for them. I know um I think it's the Big Jamaica is running bluefish and bonita trips right now. We started getting Spanish mackerel reports uh this weekend uh at the Jersey Shore. The other thing that we saw is a um Sandy Hook uh northernmost stretch of beach at the Jersey Shore had a pretty darn good bluefish blitz last week and some choppers in double-digit uh status. So, that was pretty cool. Um several weeks ago I had shared some uh drone footage from a friend of mine uh of these jumbo blues right off the beach and he didn't tell me what beach they were, but I kind of alluded the fact just hopefully at one point these bluefish will come across the bar and invade. So, apparently they've done that. Um so, that's kind of cool. So, there are things happening at this point. Our fluke bite is just starting to get better on the ocean uh lumps, ridges, uh reefs, artificial reefs especially. We had several double-digit fluke in the reports of the fishermen um this week for issue 23. Uh again on those Spanish mackerel, sheepshead from Long Beach Island south. Uh and as you mentioned Dave, yeah, the bonita. So, that's a lot more options right now in terms of what folks can target and what folks can possibly bring home. We just have to get through a week of of rain. Um if so, need an ark this week as opposed to a boat. So. >> Seriously. Uh we also saw uh an uptick in bluefish here finally. I mean, I had really haven't heard any positive bluefish news all year until this actual weekend. Um sound like some fish pushed into western Long Island Sound. I don't know if you heard the same thing Matt, but uh we had a couple shops weigh in some teen-size blues and then there was a lot of you know, just I would call like ordinary size bluefish like 5 to 7-lb blues, but um a lot of the charter captains were saying that the stripers seem to have moved uh or shifted, you know, from one location to another and the bluefish seem to appear in their place. So, it's kind of an interesting thing. But, it'll be in the sound in particular, it'll be interesting to see how how well those bluefish stick around because we got three major rivers that dump into the sound plus a bunch of, you know, lesser rivers and it just injects so much fresh water and mud and, you know, all kinds of other floating [snorts] debris and uh seems to uh really have a major effect on the fishing, especially within a few miles of each of those river mouths. >> Yeah, I did hear those bluefish show up in the sound. Um, 12, 10-lb bluefish. Central Sound, too, was seeing some. Uh also the Western Sound. So, you know, probably working on that same body of fish that you guys are working on across the pond over there, Dave. Um aside from that, I want to just um hone in on the tuna bite that's going on on the South Shore of Long Island. You know, out east off of Block Island and I again off the Jersey Shore over there, Jim. Uh I had a bunch of friends that went out. They they snuck in on that Saturday window of tuna. Uh shot out and, you know, it it there's no real concentration of these fish. Like, it's not like all the fish is set up 40 mi out or all the fish is set up 20 mi out. Cuz I had groups of friends that went out and they saw people catching 25 mi out. They dropped two on the troll. They had one on the jig that they, you know, that they lost. Had another friend, he went out, saw no life out far, came in tight, 5 mi off the beach, 80 ft of water. He sees some life. They drop down. They They jigged up like a 52, 53-in fish. >> Nice. >> So, 5 mi off the beach, you know, don't get me tempted cuz I'll take my skiff out there. But, uh yeah. Uh so, it's >> in a kayak? >> Yeah, yeah, pretty much, man. But, [clears throat] it's like, you know, if the fish are, they're not all set up on one that one line, that one fathom line. It's They're They're in close, they're far out. It's just you got to find the bait. Um you know, work that area, and hopefully you'll find some fish. Um I don't know what you guys are hearing, but that's kind of what the what I'm hearing on Long Island. I also hearing yellowfin are coming a little bit closer from the canyons. Heard as close as 40 mi out they're starting to get some yellowfin. Uh bigeye still in the canyon, white marlin still in the canyon. But um you know, those bluefin they've been It's been a scattered game. It hasn't been just one spot. It's been, you know, 25 mi and then like I said, you know, as close as 5 mi out. So, it's interesting. But I >> It's close as 5 mi from the South Shore of Long Island or 5 mi from the Jersey beaches? >> South uh South Shore of Long Island. >> All right. Good. No, cuz we're seeing this we're seeing the exact same thing. We've got bluefin tuna in as close as just a couple of miles, you know, in some instances I've heard inside state waters, you know, inside the 3-mi line. But yeah, that's That's phenomenal. That bluefin fishery is just incredible, you know, that's another one you think back 15, 20 years ago people were ringing ringing their hands and say, "Oh my god, the bluefin. We've got to We've got to do all kinds of things. We got to shut it down." And you know, that's a fishery that's really come back in amazing way. Um and you know, it's funny to think about that fish being able to travel over both sides of the Atlantic, traveling from our western Atlantic all the way across the eastern Atlantic and back again. So, It's an amazing It's an amazing amazing fishery. So, and how about those triggers? We talked a couple of weeks ago about triggerfish. Matty, are you still seeing a few along the South Shore? >> Still seeing them along the South Shore. All the major inlets have them. Fire Island, Jones, Moriches, Shinnecock. You know, the guys are going down there at the right tide. Got hopping in the right spot, soaking their clams, their pieces of squid on the bottom next just close to the rocks. They are scoring with triggerfish. Um guys on the boats, you know, if you can't get up close to the inlet rocks and anchor up or spot lock up over there. I heard the buoy chains in the bay, they're holding triggerfish as well. So, yeah, there are still triggerfish around. Actually, I do have some I have to eat still. My My friend brought me some. So, I didn't actually have to go catch some myself. But, I do have some triggerfish to eat and they have still been around. So, if you guys would love a great tasting fish with a a good fight. Yeah, hop on you know, go down to the jetty, drive your 4x4 down to the down to the inlet. Hop on the rocks, you know, get some some I and I I mentioned in my column piece recently about um triggerfishing. The one mistake I made in the past is using these these standard like a porgy rig. You know, those gold bait holder hooks. They're thin wire hooks. I can't tell you how many times I've had those triggerfish snap those hooks in half. What I like to do is I like to tie my own triggerfish rigs. And I'll use a you know, 1/0 maybe a maybe a 2/0 live bait hook. Those those thicker gauge hooks. And they won't chop them in half. I mean, I'm telling you like most times I go triggerfishing. When they get those that that mouth going and they start grinding away on that on that that metal hook. They'll they'll chop that porgy hook right in half. So, I like to I like to step up the hook gauge, go to those live bait hooks. A little tip for you if you're looking to target triggerfish out there. >> You learn more about those tips this week. I'm handed segway, right? Issue 23, I mentioned mentioned our our digital weekly edition is out this week and Matt's inshore trigger time tips. They're in this week's digital weekly edition. That's again for our subscribers. We come out every every single week and it's it's a good article and I don't take advantage of it cuz they are that's a tasty tasty species. You have a you have a few trigger fish popping up up up in New England, right Dave? >> Yeah, actually I think this I would call this week the best week of the summer so far for uh trigger fish locally. Uh the uh look the Black Hawk in in particular uh running out of Niantic, Connecticut. Uh they ran a trip earlier this week um or I middle of last week, I should say. Uh where they they basically, you know, sunk the boat with trigger fish. It was just an incredible an incredible bite of triggers and a lot just a lot of lot of reports coming from Rhode Island. Uh a lot of reports coming from some of the uh off of some of the islands of Massachusetts and even getting a little bit into Long Island Sound. Uh you know, extreme eastern Long Island Sound. Uh just a lot of those fish this year. It seems like a great year for trigger fish, for sure. Crew of the Black Hawk, of course, um real really popular with a lot of our folks in New Jersey as well. Folks go out there to to jump aboard. Great boat for kids, too, right? Absolutely fantastic. >> they take great pride in uh in introducing kids to the sport. Uh Captain Greg has been doing it for a long time. Uh I would describe him as boisterous, I guess. Um [laughter] >> In a good way. >> And yeah, no, in a in a in a very very good way. Um and uh really knows how to take a you know, a kid on board who might be nervous or you know, maybe he's new to the sport and uh just make him feel like a million bucks. So, if you're looking to get your kids out there, uh that's one of the boats that I would put at the top of the list, for sure. >> Fantastic. If you're having uh you know, we've got the opportunities to have head boats up and down the coast. Um and if you are traveling someplace, you're out of state, you know, you always have that option. I know a lot of times we're trying to figure out our travel rods, where we can sneak in time. But the best thing is those head boats give give you that opportunity to jump aboard um for half day or full day, um catch any number of species. So, definitely take advantage of that. In this week's digital edition, too, you do um another column from you, Dave, on surf the the heavier heads uh in terms of uh heavier jig bags. Why are they so important, you know, in terms of you mentioned late summer. Why is that so important this time of year? >> Well, for me and you know, this is probably something that sort of uh it's sort of plotted on a sliding scale depending on where you are geographically. So, for me, up here in New England, this bite starts a little sooner than it might in Jersey, but um it has a lot to do with bait movement, you know, coming out of the back rivers, coming out of the larger bays, coming out onto the front beaches. And a sort of taking advantage of what I refer to as a bulk up period where these stripers are they may still be resident species or they may be, you know, sort of taking a slower migration because there's not as much urgency with uh water temps not dropping precipitously. Um but you're taking advantage of a competitive situation. We have a lot of larger bait fish that are faster moving bait fish. You've got maybe a clash of some of a good size school of big striped bass and speed ends up being the the sort of the the X factor. And uh the the great equalizer, as they say. And so, what I found sort of by accident and then started to sort of do it on purpose, uh you know, the first time it worked for me, I had some jigs with lighter heads. I got snipped off by a few bluefish and I had to put the heavier one on. And you know, I had to fish it so fast because it was so light and I was in shallow enough water where I just be, you know, snagging every cast. And I mean, you would have thought I was like the Pied Piper of stripers with that with that fast moving heavy head and it's just something that I always carry now because the heavier head, you know, you have to fish it fast so it forces the issue. >> It's going to be good. >> Uh it's also really hard to bring it all the way to the surface because it's heavy and it's front weighted. Uh so you don't have that jig, you know, kicking out or rolling over on the surface. And uh it's just become one of those things that's you know, it's kind of a dummy proof system once you sort of master it because you have to reel it fast or you're going to lose it. And that extra fast uh retrieve seems to fire up these stripers at this particular time of the season. So uh heavier heads is something that stays in my bag all the time, but definitely doesn't come out every night. >> Sounds cool. The other The other feature in this week's digital weekly edition number 23 is a freshwater article by Bruce Litton, friend of mine here in New Jersey, great freshwater fisherman. Um and I think just one of the best freshwater writers one of the best writers in general, I think in the New Jersey edition. But But Bruce kind of breaks down the the idea of the popper in the chop. Uh one of my favorite things to do is throw top waters when it's windless, you have glassy conditions, you see every ripple on the surface of the water. But Bruce's reminder is sometimes those top waters even if it's not a visual strike for you as the angler, it's highly effective um in terms of targeting largemouth bass. So >> Yeah. >> Um you know, that's a kind of a huge thing. Our freshwater fishery in New Jersey is is significant. Long Island, you've got a you know, you've got a decent trout and uh and largemouth bite. And of course, New England is just ripe with with with opportunities in freshwater. So you've got a lot of lot of ground to cover for you up there in New England. >> Oh yeah. Oh yeah. It's It's funny, too, cuz when I read that um that Litton when we were in when we were in proofing um I thought about it and I was like, man, this is sort of thinking about freshwater topwater fishing as if you're fishing saltwater topwater because in the salt you're looking for chop, you know, that's when that's when your your mouth starts to water, you know, when it's flat glass calm it yeah, it can work but it's it's not as uh it's not as much of a guarantee as it is when you get a little overcast, you got some ripple on the water, maybe you got a good surf rolling in. And uh you know, you throw that pencil popper out there and I thought, you know, it's interesting that at least for me as a crossover fisherman that I never really thought of that until I read that story. So, I'm definitely going to be putting that to the test uh as we move into fall here and I do a little freshwater fishing. >> Sounds cool. Sounds cool. Crossover is big big word. We seem to we we talk about it in so many different things uh so many different fisheries. Uh it has been probably the quintessential word um in the striper fishery I think of the last 20 years. I think about the glide baits, right? The glide baits to crossover. The bunker uh the the flutter spoons a crossover. There's so many crossovers. Um especially in terms of >> Go back as far as you want to, you know, the redfin crosses over. The Slug-Go crosses over, you know, all this stuff um you know, it's just ingenuitive fisherman, you know, recognizing something and bringing it into the surf or bringing it into the inshore fishery and uh you know, it it's not a surprise that they work, you know, um predatory fish are predatory fish and it's it's it's so cool to watch it happen though over and over and over and over again. >> Those Doc Spooks, the Doc Doc is Doc is a um you know, big name in the in in those topwater um baits. That those are all musky baits, right? >> Right. Absolutely. >> Oh, I'm looking forward to the fall already. Oh, it's just uh I'm working on this week's digital weekly edition for the one that comes out in 2 weeks and I was just kind of uh kind of taking stock of where we are here in New Jersey. We're more than halfway through the summer flounder season. You know, obviously we're more than halfway uh done with with summer. So, I'm already starting to look forward to the fall. Um you guys you guys hopefully, you know, Matt, I I hope that you see those September blitzes in Montauk again the way it was in the old days. I know your fishery in in New England will be fantastic in September. We have you know, we just don't see the falls like we used to. A lot of times in the past once Labor Day came, you know, I start thinking you start getting that mindset about stripers and it seems to be just a little bit delayed. You know, we don't see that in September. We see it start sometime in early October uh our first flurries, but man, it just seems like time is passing by so fast. I blinked and summer was over. >> Mhm. >> Too fast, guys. >> I really think uh you know, I felt this in the last 5 years since coming back to the fisherman um running dead running deadlines the way that we do. You know, you're always working 2 weeks ahead of time. You're working on the next month's monthly edition. You're constantly you're constantly 2 to 4 weeks ahead of where you actually are. And that it has some positives, of course, you know, you it helps you be prepared for what's to come. But man, does it make the season go by fast? It really just makes it fly. It's you know, and if you're someone like me who really is uh so in tune to fishing the moons, that only makes it worse because as soon as one moon passes, you're like, all right, when's the next one? So, you got these deadlines, you got these moons, and the next thing you know, it's uh >> It's a fall run, man. >> Yeah, it's time to go pick out your turkey. You know what I mean? >> Yeah, that too. >> That That or we start talking about boat show season again. That's what I always love. For people realize it, we're talking about boat show season schedules in January and February, but we're not going that fast, folks. You still have plenty of time to get out there. We've talked about a lot of the options that exist here in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic. Um tuna fishery is outstanding. Just good luck getting through this week. It looks like uh I don't know. I'm I'm looking at a 10-day forecast. And rain is in the forecast just about every every day for the next 10 days. So, we'll get through this. >> On those windy days, you know, when it's uh when it's too windy to get out there and then maybe it's too rough to fish safely in the surf, that might be a good day to go try uh Litton's popper thing. That's what I'm going to try. >> Poppers in the chop in the driving rain. Yeah, it sounds like it sounds perfect. >> Yeah. >> So. Well, boys, stay dry. Have a good week. Look forward to seeing your Thursday video fishing forecast, see what's in store for the weekend ahead, but um you know. Good luck to everybody. Catch them up and uh we'll see you again next week. >> See you next week, guys.

In this booth stopover from ICAST '26, we've got a three-for-one special with exciting new product releases from the folks at Shimano.  On the lure side, Shimano's Max Dispoto shows off the Ledge Runner baits available now for both inshore and offshore trolling tactics.  Next up Benny Ortiz takes us through the Shimano Stella lineup with the brand new Stella 25000 hitting Northeast tackle shops this summer.  Finally, Shimano's John Irwin unveils the new Insurgence saltwater line of rods also available later this summer of '26. 

See the latest new releases from Shimano at https://fishshop.shimano.com/pages/2026-new-product

Thing that sets this apart that's something different than other trolling plugs, three different depth settings in the same lure. >> Really? >> So if you look right on the lip here, you have three depth settings. So you can go shallow, medium or deep, let go and it's locked in. >> You see them on the fish finder, you know where you got to drop them. It's as easy as that. >> this 160 size I've been using inshore a lot for stripers. So if I'm in shallow like say less than 20 ft and I want to keep it up high and not get hung up on the bottom, I'll run it on that shallow, but if I'm offshore a little bit in 60 or 70 ft of water and mark the fish down there, I'll switch it to the deep and run it down deep. >> Just curious, are you using this color as well? What was your favorite color for stripers? >> Um so there's six different colors right now. The pink has a time and place. Some days they like it cuz it sticks out a lot and then there's a flyer flash that's a natural bait fish color. I usually start the day off with one of each and see which one that they like that day. So >> So you're moving in and out of the canyon, maybe put it down a little bit and see if you can't get that wahoo on the edge. >> Exactly, exactly. Every one of these swims perfectly straight off the package. Has this hydro control wing here, stabilizes the lure kind of like a spoiler or the wings of a plane. Keeps the water running straight on it so it won't kick left, kick right, fly out of the water on you. >> Look for these right away, right? >> Yeah, they're available now. Yeah. >> Let's go find out from Benny Ortiz what's new on the reel side. >> Sounds good. >> Benny Ortiz, what's happening? >> Good to see you. >> Good to see you. I've been anxious to come over here to look at the brand new Stella. >> That's right. Here she is. This is the Stella 25,000. So this fills the gap between the 20 and the 30K size because the 30K that's a beast of a reel with very limited applications. This one very more a little bit more versatile with still in that same capacity of fish and same quality of fish. So you're thinking throwing big plugs, big stick baits, jigging deep water, big pelagic fish. That's what this is designed for. So couple of upgrades that we did with this model. Biggest thing we'll start on the top of the reel, we'll work our way down. We have our double X tough drag in here. Drag washer was moved to the top of the reel, also enlarged so you have that cross carbon drag on here which puts out an amazing 66 lb of drag which is incredible. Most humans can't even hold on to 66 lb, you know? Um inside here we have our heat sink drag. What that does is it doesn't change the amount of heat that's in the reel but it changes where the heat goes. So instead of being targeted here and near your the bottom of your spool, it gets dissipated into the body of the reel. That reduces the heat up to 30%. So no more pouring water on reels to try to keep them cool, no more melting drag when you're fishing for melting line when you're fishing for bluefin, that kind of stuff. Internally, we sealed it up in all the right spots but didn't put too much to stop that super smooth handle turn. I'm going to give that to you. Absolutely buttery smooth, just what you would expect from a Stella, and this is just a beast. The freshwater guys are totally familiar with it. It gives that rod just a extra added sensitivity. >> Just feels really good. Like with so many rods, it's just light. You know you can trust it. The Insurgent from Shimano. And this is a full 2026 release, I believe. >> Yes. We have 10 spinning and three casting actions all the way up to tarpon. And in the casting casting is a little bit more of a utility. It's not necessarily like a short grip or something that the Texas guys might like as much, but it is just a general all around three casting rods in three different actions, a light, a medium, and a heavy. >> You mentioned tarpon. If you're looking for a striper rod this fall for throwing some of those smaller top waters, those little little tiny spook stick baits, or maybe some soft plastics, definitely give the Insurgent a shot. >> Fuji guides, tangle-free Fuji guides, and the spiral X technology of the rod. >> Kind of retail price are we looking at this? >> So, 329 up to 349. >> Fantastic. Think these will be popular. Good luck with this, John. >> Yeah, thanks. >> [music]

Seven species, 70 leaderboard spots, and one Steiger Craft grand prize—the 2026 Dream Boat Fishing Challenge gets underway May 1st.

Every fishing season has its moments. The first spring blackfish that thumps a jig in chilly April water. A fluke drifting across a sandy edge in July. The unmistakable run of a big bluefish cutting through a late-summer tide. Those moments are what keep anglers coming back to the water year after year. For many fishermen, those experiences are reward enough. But for a dedicated group of anglers across the Northeast, the season carries an added element of competition.

Each year, subscribers to The Fisherman Magazine have the opportunity to take part in one of the region’s most unique and challenging fishing c…

all_videos_in_window.title: "The Best Time to Fish Is Anytime You Can" — Pete Utschig on fishing travel - Saltwater Edge Podcast
all_videos_in_window.description:
Pete Utschig of Phase Gear — the surfcaster behind Project Magic Hour and the Surfcasters documentary series — joins Peter Jenkins in Newport, mid-way through a two-week run up the coast from Florida.

Pete explains how a single weekend trip 15 years ago turned Florida's beaches into his home water, how an Airbnb guide service grew into a full all-inclusive surf fishing lodge (December–April, rods, lures, and food included — bring board shorts), and why his bucket list is made of fish, not places: cubera snapper, giant trevally in Indonesia, corvina in Ecuador, giant tarpon in Gabon, and bluefin tuna from the rocks in Europe. Plus the philosophy that holds it all together: you can't control the tides, but you can control the vibes — and the best time to fish is anytime you can.

raw_posts.title: Fri Aug 7 – Whale Watching
raw_posts.content: A 5-species cetacean day! On our travels offshore to find the humpbacks we encountered on Wednesday’s trip, we discovered numerous small pods of Tamanend’s bottlenose dolphins which could be seen swimming through the swells and waves around our vessel about 3 miles from the lighthouse. The dolphins were not at all bothered by our presence, and could be seen in all directions around our vessel affording passengers excellent views. Continuing offshore, we saw a tremendous breach from miles away and at least one spout, but the whales were on the move and we, at first, only encountered a small finback whale. We continued on, encountering numerous small pods of short-beaked common dolphin, which would approach the vessel and swim beneath our bow to the excitement of the passengers. No humpbacks were spotted in their previous locations or to the west,…

raw_posts.title: Sun July 19 – Whale Watching
raw_posts.content: EPIC whale watching with CRESLI and the Viking Fleet! This season continues to bring passengers to an absolute ‘whale wonderland’, with multiple cetacean species, large numbers of whales, and incredible encounters. Yesterday was no exception as we sailed through crisp, clear skies, a wonderful reprieve from the wildfire smoke that had previously plagued the region….

raw_posts.title: Mon July 27 – Whale Watching
raw_posts.content: “World Class Whale Watching” with the Viking Fleet! To put today’s whale watch into perspective, it helps to explain how we found three cetacean species early on and decided to leave them in search of something more. A few miles after passing Montauk Point lighthouse, we encountered a juvenile humpback feeding at depth with glimpses of a minke whale and a couple of Tamanend’s bottlenose dolphin. Although we stuck around for a bit hoping for better views, we decided to continue south and search for some of the adult humpbacks encountered on yesterday’s trip. It didn’t take long before we could see whales breaking the surface of the water and spouts soon filled the horizon. Those blows belonged to over a dozen humpback cooperatively bubble net feeding in groups of 2,3, and 7. With excellent views of the action, we…

all_videos.description:
Lights out marlin fishing in the Mid-Atlantic, bluefin fishing finally getting good in New England, and have Jimmy and Cheech caught a tuna yet? Spoiler Alert: No.

We cover:

🎣 Bluefin & Yellowfin Tuna

60–70-inch recreational fish showing up on jigs
Yellowfin mixing with bluefin from New Jersey through Southern New England
Live squid and slow-worked soft plastics producing
Big bluefin still being caught on live bait
The latest reports from Montauk, Long Island, and New Jersey

🌊 Canyon Fishing

Yellowfin concentrating around specific water-temperature and chlorophyll edges
Shorter trips producing multiple fish
Marlin and mahi becoming increasingly important offshore
What the new moon could mean for the canyon bite

🐟 Gulf of Maine

Bluefin action heating back up
60–70-inch fish mixed in …

all_videos.title: GIANTS everywhere | Northeast Offshore Fishing Report August 5th, 2026
all_videos.description:
In this week's Northeast Offshore Fishing Report, Anthony DeiCicchi and Liam O'Neill break down the epic giant bluefin tuna fishing off Cape Cod, where monster tuna continue to feed aggressively. Meanwhile, recreational-sized bluefin tuna have become much harder to find east of Montauk.

The world's largest billfish tournament, the White Marlin Open, returns August 3–8. Deane Lambrose of Canyon Runner shares the latest offshore fishing report from Ocean City, Maryland, including updates on tuna, marlin, and other offshore action.

all_videos.description:
Cape Cod Bay Bass & Bluefin with Sam Mullen of the Goose Hummock | Early August Fishing Report

Sam Mullen of the Goose Hummock in Orleans joins Kevin Collins for an early August fishing report covering Cape Cod Bay and beyond. Cape Cod Bay is still the star of the show for striped bass — and the squid bite is still ripping. Bluefish are finally filtering in. Bonito have arrived in the bay. And Sam shares the incredible story of landing a 485-pound giant bluefin on a 21-foot center console. Plus a full bottom fish update: fluke, sea bass, and the late-season sea bass extension through October 14th.

all_videos.title: Great White Shark Bites Striped Bass in Half
all_videos.description:
This one was sent to us by F/V Three Little Birds. Back on June 13th at Handkerchief Shoal, off Monomoy Island — a great white shark tracked, then struck a striped bass clean in half.⁠
⁠
Handkerchief Shoal is a shifting sandbar at the edge of Nantucket Sound, notorious for strong currents and shallow water that's made it treacherous for boats for centuries — but that same water has also made it one of the most productive striper and bluefish grounds on Cape Cod. Apparently the great whites know it too.⁠

all_videos.description:
July produced a hot squid bite offshore at the canyons for MFCC group trip captain Willy Hatch of Machaca Charters. The lights pulled in an entire ecosystem — you can see the baitfish balled up tight against the boat, with squid working them over, all lit up right off the boat. ⁠
⁠
The crew jigged some up, and even scooped a few straight out of the water with a dip net. Offshore trips like this aren't just about the tuna — nights like these remind you how much is happening beneath the surface that most people never get to see.⁠

all_videos.title: Bass Attack a Paddletail Underwater (Slowed Down 80%)
all_videos.description:
Just a little more Monomoy Tackle paddletail action for ya. Filmed earlier this summer off Wellfleet onboard one of our weekly MFCC trips with Flatliner Charters. These bass were moving fast, so we slowed the footage down by as much as 80% — at real speed, these strikes happen in the blink of an eye.

A few people have asked how we got this one — I used a WaterWolf in-line camera with the paddletail rigged about 3 feet out in front of it. Tyler would bring me right up to the blitzes, I would cast towards the edge of the commotion, and reel the paddle at a pretty fast clip since the bass were really focused on the surface. 

Wish I could take credit for perfect timing, but a lot of this comes down to getting lucky and being in the right place at the right time. 🎣

Tight lines! 🎣

Ryan

all_videos.title: August 6th, 2026 New Jersey/Delaware Bay Fishing Report with Jim Hutchinson, Jr.
all_videos.description: Some quality fluke reported out of the Shark River Inlet fleet in the past week is evidence enough of an improving bite out along the inshore sticky stuff.  We'll run down a few of the latest catches reported back to us here at The Fisherman Magazine for the New Jersey, Delaware Bay region, with fluke, sheepshead, and blowfish, perhaps backed up with a steamer-full of little necks (6:40).  Run through the August editorial lineup in the magazine, and our digital weekly (10:12) with an overview of this week's Next Cast and the connection between rays, cobia and bluefin tuna along with the latest offshore intel from Canyon Runner.  Our lead image of the week (22:10) puts a husband and wife in the right spot at the time for their wedding anniversary and a blitz of bluefish at Sandy Hook as we …

all_videos.description: This week's Long Island Video Fishing Forecast comes from Island Yacht's new marina in Bay Shore, where we take a tour of the facility with Chet before diving into another action-packed fishing report. We preview new Daiwa and Tsunami gear from ICAST, plug Episode 20 of The Fisherman Podcast—covering the booming shark bite, nearshore bluefin tuna, triggerfish tactics, and menhaden management—and bring you the latest Canyon Runner offshore update. Around the Island, anglers are enjoying steady fluke action, quality bluefin tuna, bull sharks, sheepshead, striped bass, Spanish mackerel, mahi, and more, highlighted by great catches from both boats and the surf. We also feature Dream Boat Challenge updates, magazine previews, a new correspondent segment with Mark Sedotti on crushing barbs for s…

Fall 26 for these guys. >> Obviously, the SP Minnow has become the quintessential lure. Seven species, 70 leaderboard spots, and one Steiger Craft grand prize—the 2026 Dream Boat Fishing Challenge gets underway May 1st.

Every fishing season has its moments. The first spring blackfish that thumps a jig in chilly April water. A fluke drifting across a sandy edge in July. all_videos.title: "The Best Time to Fish Is Anytime You Can" — Pete Utschig on fishing travel - Saltwater Edge Podcast
all_videos.description:
Pete Utschig of Phase Gear — the surfcaster behind Project Magic Hour and the Surfcasters documentary series — joins Peter Jenkins in Newport, mid-way through a two-week run up the coast from Florida.

Pete explains how a single weekend trip 15 years ago turned Florida's beaches into his home water, how an Airbnb guide service grew into a full all-inclusive surf fishing lodge (December–April, rods, lures, and food included — bring board shorts), and why his bucket list is made of fish, not places: cubera snapper, giant trevally in Indonesia, corvina in Ecuador, giant tarpon in Gabon, and bluefin tuna from the rocks in Europe. Plus the philosophy that holds it all together: you can't control the tides, but you can control the vibes — and the best time to fish is anytime you can.
